chapters.title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 16
paragraphs: Suddenly there was a stir — everyone began talking and pressing forward and then stepping back — and between the two rows that parted, the Emperor entered to music that struck up at once. Behind him walked his host and hostess. He walked in quickly, bowing to right and left as if eager to get the first moments of the reception over with. The band played the polonaise that was popular at the time, with its well-known words beginning: "Alexander, Elisaveta, all our hearts you ravish quite..." The Emperor passed on into the drawing room, the crowd surged toward the doors, and several people with excited faces hurried there and back again. Then the crowd quickly pulled back from the drawing room door as the Emperor reappeared talking to the hostess. A young man looking flustered swooped down on the ladies, asking them to move aside. Some women, their faces betraying complete forgetfulness of all decorum, pushed forward at the expense of their dresses. The men began choosing partners and taking their places for the polonaise.

Everyone moved back, and the Emperor came smiling out of the drawing room, leading his hostess by the hand but not keeping time with the music. The host followed with Marya Antonovna Naryshkina; then came ambassadors, ministers, and various generals, whom Peronskaya diligently named. More than half the ladies already had partners and were taking up, or preparing to take up, their positions for the polonaise. Natasha felt that she would be left with her mother and Sonya among a minority of women clustered near the wall who had not been asked to dance. She stood with her slender arms hanging down, her barely formed chest rising and falling evenly, holding her breath, her eyes glittering with fright as she stared straight ahead — ready for either the greatest joy or deepest misery. She wasn't thinking about the Emperor or any of those important people Peronskaya kept pointing out — she had only one thought: "Is it possible that nobody will ask me, that I won't be among the first to dance? Is it possible that none of all these men will notice me? They don't even seem to see me, and if they do, they look as though they're thinking, 'Ah, she's not the one I'm after, so she's not worth looking at!' No, it's impossible," she thought. "They must know how much I want to dance, how wonderfully I dance, and how much they would enjoy dancing with me."

The strains of the polonaise, which had been going on for quite some time, had begun to sound like a sad memory to Natasha's ears. She wanted to cry. Peronskaya had left them. The count was at the other end of the room. She and the countess and Sonya stood there by themselves as if in the depths of a forest amid that crowd of strangers, with no one interested in them, no one wanting them. Prince Andrew passed by with a lady on his arm, clearly not recognizing them. The handsome Anatole stood smiling as he talked to his partner and glanced at Natasha the way one glances at a wall. Boris passed them twice and each time looked away. Berg and his wife, who weren't dancing, came up to them.

This family gathering felt humiliating to Natasha — as if there were nowhere else for the family to talk but here at the ball. She didn't listen to or look at Vera, who was telling her something about her own green dress.

At last the Emperor stopped beside his final partner — he had danced with three — and the music stopped. A concerned aide-de-camp ran up to the Rostovs asking them to stand further back, though they were already practically against the wall, and from the gallery came the clear, precise, irresistibly rhythmic strains of a waltz. The Emperor looked down the room with a smile. A minute passed but no one had begun to dance. An aide-de-camp, the Master of Ceremonies, went up to Countess Bezukhova and invited her to dance. She raised her hand with a smile and placed it on his shoulder without looking at him. The aide-de-camp, an expert in his craft, grasped his partner firmly around the waist and with confident precision started gliding smoothly, first around the edge of the circle, then at the corner of the room he caught Helene's left hand and spun her — the only sounds, aside from the ever-quickening music, being the rhythmic click of his spurs on his quick, nimble feet, while at every third beat his partner's velvet dress flared out and seemed to flash as she whirled around. Natasha watched them and was ready to cry because it wasn't she dancing that first turn of the waltz.

Prince Andrew, in the white uniform of a cavalry colonel, wearing stockings and dancing shoes, stood looking animated and bright in the front row of the circle, not far from the Rostovs. Baron Firhoff was talking to him about the first session of the Council of State that was to be held the next day. Prince Andrew, as someone closely connected to Speransky and involved in the work of the legislative commission, could provide reliable information about that session, about which various rumors were circulating. But he wasn't listening to Firhoff — he was looking now at the sovereign and now at the men who meant to dance but hadn't yet worked up the courage to step into the circle.
Prince Andrew was watching these men, intimidated by the Emperor's presence, and the women who were breathlessly longing to be asked to dance.
Pierre came up to him and caught him by the arm.
"You always dance. I have a protegee here — the young Rostova. Ask her," he said.

"Where is she?" asked Bolkonski. "Excuse me!" he added, turning to the baron, "we'll finish this conversation elsewhere — at a ball one must dance." He stepped forward in the direction Pierre had indicated. The despairing, dejected expression on Natasha's face caught his eye. He recognized her, guessed her feelings, saw that this was her debut, remembered their conversation at the window, and with an expression of pleasure approached Countess Rostova.
"Allow me to introduce you to my daughter," said the countess, her face flushing.

"I have the pleasure of being already acquainted, if the countess remembers me," said Prince Andrew with a low and courteous bow that completely contradicted Peronskaya's remarks about his rudeness. Approaching Natasha, he held out his arm to take her waist before he had even finished his invitation. He asked her to waltz. That trembling expression on Natasha's face, poised between despair and ecstasy, suddenly broke into a happy, grateful, childlike smile.

"I've been waiting for you so long," that frightened, happy little girl seemed to say through the smile that replaced the threatened tears, as she raised her hand to Prince Andrew's shoulder. They were the second couple to enter the circle. Prince Andrew was one of the finest dancers of his day, and Natasha danced exquisitely. Her small feet in their white satin shoes moved swiftly, lightly, and as if of their own accord, while her face beamed with ecstatic happiness. Her slender bare arms and neck were not classically beautiful — compared to Helene's, her shoulders looked thin and her figure undeveloped. But Helene seemed hardened by a kind of varnish, the residue of thousands of gazes that had appraised her, while Natasha was like a girl exposed for the first time, who would have felt deeply embarrassed had she not been assured that this was absolutely proper.

Prince Andrew liked dancing, and wishing to escape as quickly as possible from the political and intellectual conversation everyone kept directing at him, and wishing also to break through the circle of formality he found stifling under the Emperor's presence, he danced — and he had chosen Natasha because Pierre pointed her out and because she was the first pretty girl who caught his eye. But no sooner had he put his arm around that slender, supple waist and felt her moving so close to him, smiling so near — than the wine of her charm went to his head, and he felt himself revived and rejuvenated. After leaving her he stood breathing deeply, watching the other dancers.

chapters.title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 17
paragraphs: After Prince Andrew, Boris came up to ask Natasha for a dance, and then the aide-de-camp who had opened the ball, and several other young men, so that, flushed and happy, passing off her extra partners to Sonya, she danced without stopping all evening. She noticed nothing of what occupied everyone else. Not only did she fail to see that the Emperor had a long conversation with the French ambassador, or that he was especially gracious to a certain lady, or that Prince So-and-so did this and So-and-so said that, or that Helene was a great success and received special attention from Such-and-such — she didn't even see the Emperor, and only realized he'd left because the ball became livelier after his departure. During one of the merry cotillions before supper, Prince Andrew was her partner again. He reminded her of their first meeting in the avenue at Otradnoe and how she had been unable to sleep that moonlit night, and told her how he had accidentally overheard her. Natasha blushed at the memory and tried to excuse herself, as if there had been something to be ashamed of in what Prince Andrew had overheard.

Like all men who have grown up in society, Prince Andrew enjoyed meeting someone who didn't conform to the standard social mold. And such was Natasha, with her surprise, her delight, her shyness, and even her occasional mistakes in French. With her he was especially careful and tender, sitting beside her and talking about the simplest and most trivial things, admiring her shy grace. In the middle of the cotillion, having completed one of the figures, Natasha, still out of breath, was returning to her seat when another dancer chose her. She was tired and panting and clearly thought of declining, but immediately put her hand gaily on the man's shoulder, smiling at Prince Andrew.

"I'd love to sit beside you and rest — I'm tired; but you see how they keep asking me, and I'm glad of it, I'm happy, and I love everybody, and you and I understand all of it" — and much, much more was said in her smile. When her partner released her, Natasha ran across the room to choose two ladies for the figure.
"If she goes to her cousin first and then to another lady, she will be my wife," said Prince Andrew to himself, quite to his own surprise, as he watched her. She did go first to her cousin.

"What nonsense sometimes enters one's head!" thought Prince Andrew. "But one thing is certain — that girl is so charming, so original, that she won't be dancing here a month before she'll be engaged... Girls like her are rare here," he thought, as Natasha, readjusting a rose that was slipping on her bodice, settled down beside him.

When the cotillion ended, the old count in his blue coat came up to the dancers. He invited Prince Andrew to visit them and asked his daughter if she was enjoying herself. Natasha didn't answer at once but only looked up with a smile that said reproachfully: "How can you even ask?"

"I have never enjoyed myself so much!" she said, and Prince Andrew noticed how her thin arms rose quickly as if to embrace her father and instantly dropped again. Natasha was happier than she had ever been in her life. She was at that peak of bliss where one becomes completely kind and good and cannot believe in the possibility of evil, unhappiness, or sorrow.

At that ball Pierre felt for the first time humiliated by the position his wife occupied in court circles. He was gloomy and distracted. A deep furrow ran across his forehead, and standing by a window he stared through his spectacles, seeing no one.
On her way to supper Natasha passed him.
Pierre's gloomy, unhappy expression struck her. She stopped in front of him. She wanted to help him, to share the overflowing abundance of her own happiness.
"How wonderful it is, Count!" she said. "Isn't it?"
Pierre smiled absently, clearly not grasping what she had said.
"Yes, I'm very glad," he said.

"How can anyone be unhappy about anything?" thought Natasha. "Especially such a fine person as Bezukhov!" In Natasha's eyes all the people at the ball were equally good, kind, and wonderful — people who loved one another, none of them capable of hurting anyone else — and so they all ought to be happy.

chapters.title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 18
paragraphs: The next day Prince Andrew thought about the ball, but his mind didn't linger on it long. "Yes, it was a very brilliant ball," and then... "Yes, that little Rostova is very charming. There's something fresh, original, un-Petersburg-like about her that sets her apart." That was all he thought about the previous evening's ball, and after his morning tea he set to work.
But either from fatigue or lack of sleep he was in no mood for work and couldn't get anything done. He kept criticizing his own work, as he often did, and was glad when he heard someone arriving.

The visitor was Bitski, who served on various committees, frequented all the societies in Petersburg, was a passionate devotee of new ideas and of Speransky, and was a tireless Petersburg gossip — one of those men who choose their opinions the way they choose their clothes, following the latest fashion, but who for that very reason seem to be the most fervent partisans of all. He had barely gotten rid of his hat before he rushed into Prince Andrew's room with a preoccupied air and started talking at once. He had just heard the details of that morning's opening session of the Council of State by the Emperor, and he spoke of it with great enthusiasm. The Emperor's speech had been extraordinary — a speech only a constitutional monarch could deliver. "The Sovereign said plainly that the Council and Senate are estates of the realm; he said that government must rest not on authority but on secure foundations. The Emperor said the fiscal system must be reorganized and the public accounts published," Bitski reported, emphasizing certain words and opening his eyes significantly.
"Ah, yes! Today's events mark an epoch — the greatest epoch in our history," he concluded.

Prince Andrew listened to the account of the Council of State's opening — which he had awaited so impatiently and to which he had attached such importance — and was surprised that this event, now that it had actually taken place, didn't affect him at all and even seemed quite trivial. He listened with quiet irony to Bitski's enthusiastic account. A very simple thought occurred to him: "What does it matter to me or to Bitski what the Emperor chose to say at the Council? Can any of that make me happier or better?"

And this simple reflection suddenly destroyed all the interest Prince Andrew had felt in the upcoming reforms. He was supposed to dine that evening at Speransky's — "with just a few friends," as the host had said when inviting him. The prospect of dinner in the intimate home circle of the man he so admired had greatly interested Prince Andrew, especially since he had never seen Speransky in his domestic surroundings. But now he felt disinclined to go.

At the appointed hour, however, he entered the modest house Speransky owned in the Taurida Gardens. In the parquet-floored dining room of this small house — remarkable for its extreme cleanliness, almost like a monastery — Prince Andrew, who arrived rather late, found the friendly gathering of Speransky's close associates already assembled for the five o'clock meal. There were no ladies present except Speransky's little daughter — long-faced like her father — and her governess. The other guests were Gervais, Magnitsky, and Stolypin. While still in the front hall Prince Andrew heard loud voices and a ringing staccato laugh — a laugh like one hears on stage. Someone — it sounded like Speransky — was unmistakably erupting in ha-ha-ha's. Prince Andrew had never before heard Speransky's famous laugh, and this ringing, high-pitched laughter from a statesman made a strange impression on him.

He entered the dining room. The entire company was standing between two windows at a small table set with appetizers. Speransky, wearing a gray tailcoat with a star on the breast and evidently still in the same waistcoat and high white stock he had worn at the Council session, stood at the table with a beaming face. His guests surrounded him. Magnitsky, addressing Speransky, was telling an anecdote, and Speransky was laughing in advance at what Magnitsky was about to say. When Prince Andrew entered, Magnitsky's words were again crowned with laughter. Stolypin gave a deep bass guffaw as he munched bread and cheese. Gervais laughed softly with a hissing chuckle, and Speransky in his high-pitched staccato way.
Still laughing, Speransky held out his soft white hand to Prince Andrew.

"Delighted to see you, Prince," he said. "One moment..." he went on, turning to Magnitsky and interrupting his story. "We've agreed that this is a dinner for relaxation, with not a word about business!" And turning back to the storyteller he began to laugh again.

Prince Andrew looked at the laughing Speransky with astonishment, regret, and disillusionment. It seemed to him that this was not Speransky but someone else entirely. Everything that had formerly appeared mysterious and fascinating in Speransky suddenly became plain and unattractive.

At dinner the conversation never paused for a moment and seemed to consist of entries from a book of funny stories. Before Magnitsky had finished one anecdote, someone else was eager to tell something even funnier. Most of the stories, if not about the civil service directly, were about people in government. It seemed that in this company the insignificance of such people was so firmly established that the only possible attitude toward them was amused mockery. Speransky told how a deaf dignitary at the Council that morning, when asked for his opinion, had replied that he thought so too. Gervais gave a long account of an official inspection, remarkable for the stupidity of everyone involved. Stolypin, stuttering, broke into the conversation and began talking heatedly about administrative abuses under the old system — threatening to make things serious. Magnitsky started teasing Stolypin about his passionate tone. Gervais stepped in with a joke, and the talk reverted to its former lively character.

Evidently Speransky liked to relax after his labors and enjoy himself among friends, and his guests, understanding this, tried to entertain him and amuse themselves. But their gaiety struck Prince Andrew as forced and joyless. Speransky's high-pitched voice grated on him, and the incessant laughter felt like a false note. Prince Andrew didn't laugh and feared he was dampening the mood, but no one seemed to notice that he was out of step with the general atmosphere. They all appeared very merry.
He tried several times to join in the conversation, but each time his remarks were tossed aside like a cork thrown out of water, and he couldn't joke along with them.

There was nothing wrong or improper in what they said — it was clever and might have been funny — but it lacked that certain something which is the true spirit of humor, and they weren't even aware that such a thing existed.
After dinner Speransky's daughter and her governess got up. He patted the little girl with his white hand and kissed her. And that gesture, too, seemed unnatural to Prince Andrew.

The men stayed at the table over their port, in the English fashion. In the middle of a conversation about Napoleon's affairs in Spain, which they all agreed in approving, Prince Andrew began to voice a contrary opinion. Speransky smiled and, clearly wishing to steer the conversation away from an awkward turn, told a story that had nothing to do with what they'd been discussing. For a few moments everyone was silent.

After sitting at the table for a while longer, Speransky corked a bottle of wine and, remarking, "Good wine travels in style these days," handed it to the servant and stood up. Everyone rose and, still talking loudly, moved into the drawing room. Two letters brought by a courier were handed to Speransky and he took them to his study. As soon as he left the room, the general merriment stopped and the guests began to converse in a sensible, quiet way.

"Now for the recitation!" said Speransky on returning from his study. "A wonderful talent!" he said to Prince Andrew, and Magnitsky immediately struck a pose and began reciting some humorous French verses he had written about various well-known Petersburg figures. He was interrupted several times by applause. When the verses were finished, Prince Andrew went up to Speransky and took his leave.
"Where are you off to so early?" asked Speransky.
"I promised to go to a reception."

They said no more. Prince Andrew looked closely into those mirror-like, impenetrable eyes and felt that it had been absurd of him to have expected anything from Speransky, or from any of his own activities connected with him, or ever to have attributed importance to what Speransky was doing. That precise, humorless laugh rang in Prince Andrew's ears long after he had left the house.

When he got home, Prince Andrew began thinking about his life in Petersburg during those last four months as if it were something completely new. He recalled his efforts, his solicitations, and the history of his army reform project, which had been accepted for consideration but which they were trying to bury in silence simply because another, much worse proposal had already been prepared and submitted to the Emperor. He thought of the committee meetings Berg was part of. He remembered how carefully and at what length everything relating to form and procedure was discussed at those meetings, and how studiously everything relating to the actual substance of the work was avoided. He recalled his work on the Legal Code, and how painstakingly he had translated articles from the Roman and French codes into Russian, and he felt ashamed of himself. Then he vividly pictured Bogucharovo, his activities in the country, his trip to Ryazan; he remembered the peasants and Dron the village elder, and mentally applying to them the section on Personal Rights he had divided into paragraphs, he was astonished that he could have spent so much time on such useless work.

chapters.title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 19
paragraphs: The next day Prince Andrew made calls at several houses he had not previously visited, including the Rostovs', with whom he had renewed his acquaintance at the ball. Apart from considerations of politeness that required the visit, he wanted to see that original, eager girl who had left such a pleasant impression on him — this time in her own home.

Natasha was one of the first to greet him. She was wearing a dark blue house dress in which Prince Andrew thought her even prettier than in her ball gown. She and the entire Rostov family welcomed him as an old friend — simply and warmly. The whole family, whom he had formerly judged harshly, now seemed to him to consist of excellent, straightforward, and kindly people. The old count's hospitality and good nature, which in Petersburg came as a particularly pleasant surprise, were such that Prince Andrew could not refuse to stay for dinner. "Yes," he thought, "they are wonderful people who of course have no idea what a treasure they possess in Natasha; but they are kind folk and make the best possible setting for this strikingly poetic, charming girl, so full of life!"

In Natasha, Prince Andrew sensed a strange world completely unlike his own, brimming with joys he had never known — a different world that had already begun to unsettle him in the Otradnoe avenue and at the window that moonlit night. Now this world no longer unsettled him and was no longer foreign; having entered it himself, he found in it a new kind of pleasure.

After dinner, at Prince Andrew's request, Natasha went to the clavichord and began to sing. Prince Andrew stood by a window talking to the ladies and listened to her. In the middle of a sentence he stopped speaking and suddenly felt tears rising in his throat — something he had thought impossible for him. He looked at Natasha as she sang, and something new and joyful stirred in his soul. He felt happy and at the same time sad. He had absolutely no reason to cry, yet he was on the verge of tears. About what? His former love? The little princess? His disillusionment? His hopes for the future? Yes and no. The main thing was a sudden, vivid awareness of the terrible contrast between something infinitely vast and boundless within him and the limited, material thing that he — and even she — actually was. This contrast weighed on him and yet lifted him while she sang.

As soon as Natasha finished, she went up to him and asked how he liked her voice. She asked this and then grew confused, feeling she shouldn't have asked. He smiled, looking at her, and said he liked her singing as he liked everything she did.

Prince Andrew left the Rostovs' late that evening. He went to bed from habit but soon realized he could not sleep. Having lit his candle he sat up in bed, then got up, then lay down again, not at all bothered by his sleeplessness: his soul was as fresh and joyful as if he had stepped out of a stuffy room into God's own open air. It didn't occur to him that he was falling in love with Natasha; he wasn't thinking about her directly, but only picturing her to himself — and as a result, all of life appeared in a new light. "Why do I struggle, why do I toil in this narrow, confined frame, when life — all life, with all its joys — lies open before me?" he said to himself. And for the first time in a very long while he began making happy plans for the future. He decided he must attend to his son's education by finding a tutor and entrusting the boy to his care, then he should retire from the service and go abroad — see England, Switzerland, and Italy. "I must make use of my freedom while I feel so much strength and youth in me," he told himself. "Pierre was right when he said one must believe in the possibility of happiness in order to be happy, and now I do believe in it. Let the dead bury their dead — while one has life, one must live and be happy!" he thought.

chapters.title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 20
paragraphs: One morning Colonel Berg, whom Pierre knew as he knew everybody in Moscow and Petersburg, came to see him. Berg arrived in a spotless new uniform, with his hair slicked and brushed forward over his temples the way Emperor Alexander wore his.
"I've just been to see the countess, your wife. Unfortunately she couldn't grant my request, but I hope, Count, I shall have better luck with you," he said with a smile.
"What can I do for you, Colonel? I'm at your service."

"I have now completely settled into my new rooms, Count" — Berg said this with perfect conviction that this information could only be welcome — "and so I would like to arrange a small gathering for my wife's and my friends." He smiled even more pleasantly. "I would like to ask the countess and you to do me the honor of coming for tea and supper."

Only Countess Helene, who considered the company of people like the Bergs beneath her, could be cruel enough to refuse such an invitation. Berg explained so clearly why he wanted to assemble a small but select group at his home, and why this would give him pleasure, and why — though he hated spending money on cards or anything wasteful — he was prepared to incur some expense for the sake of good company, that Pierre couldn't refuse and promised to come.

"But please don't be late, Count, if I may ask — about ten minutes to eight, please. We'll set up a card game. Our general is coming. He's been very kind to me. We'll have supper, Count. So you'll do me the honor."
Contrary to his habit of being late, Pierre arrived at the Bergs' house that day not at ten but at fifteen minutes to eight.
Having prepared everything needed for the party, the Bergs were ready for their guests' arrival.

In their new, clean, well-lit study, with its small busts and pictures and new furniture, sat Berg and his wife. Berg, tightly buttoned in his new uniform, sat beside his wife explaining that one can and should always cultivate acquaintances with people above one's own station, because only then does one get real satisfaction from social connections.

"You can learn something, you can ask for something. Look at how I've advanced since my first promotion." Berg measured his life not by years but by promotions. "My former comrades are still nobodies, while I'm just waiting for a regimental command and have the happiness of being your husband." He rose and kissed Vera's hand, pausing on the way to straighten a turned-up corner of the carpet. "And how did I achieve all this? Mainly by knowing how to choose my acquaintances. It goes without saying that one must be conscientious and methodical."

Berg smiled with a sense of superiority over his weak-natured wife and paused, reflecting that this dear wife of his was after all only a weak woman who could not understand everything that constitutes a man's dignity — what it means to be a man (in German). Vera, at the same time, smiled with a sense of superiority over her good, conscientious husband, who nevertheless understood life incorrectly, as in Vera's view all men did. Berg, judging by his wife, thought all women weak and foolish. Vera, judging by her husband alone and generalizing from that, believed that all men, though they understand nothing and are conceited and selfish, credit only themselves with common sense.
* ein Mann zu sein.
Berg rose and carefully embraced his wife, so as not to crush her lace collar, for which he had paid a good price, and kissed her squarely on the lips.
"The only thing is — we mustn't have children too soon," he added, following an unconscious chain of thought.
"Yes," answered Vera, "I don't want that at all. We must live for society."
"Princess Yusupova wore one exactly like this," said Berg, pointing to the lace collar with a happy and kindly smile.
Just then Count Bezukhov was announced. Husband and wife exchanged glances, both smiling with self-satisfaction, each mentally claiming the credit for this visit.
"This is what comes of knowing how to cultivate acquaintances," thought Berg. "This is what comes of knowing how to conduct oneself."
"But please don't interrupt me when I'm entertaining the guests," said Vera, "because I know what interests each of them and what to say to different people."
Berg smiled again.
"It can't be helped — men must sometimes have masculine conversation," he said.

They received Pierre in their small, new drawing room, where it was impossible to sit down anywhere without disrupting the symmetry, neatness, and order; so it was perfectly understandable — and not at all strange — that Berg, having generously offered to sacrifice the arrangement of an armchair or the sofa for his dear guest, yet being obviously tormented by indecision himself, left it to the visitor to solve the seating problem. Pierre disrupted the symmetry by pulling over a chair, and Berg and Vera immediately launched into their evening party, each interrupting the other in their eagerness to entertain their guest.

Vera, having decided that Pierre ought to be entertained with conversation about the French embassy, began accordingly. Berg, having decided that masculine conversation was called for, interrupted his wife to raise the question of the war with Austria, and before he knew it had veered from the general topic to personal matters — the offers he'd received to take part in the Austrian campaign and the reasons he had declined them. Though the conversation was thoroughly disjointed and Vera was annoyed at the intrusion of the masculine element, both husband and wife felt with satisfaction that, even with only one guest present, their evening had begun very well and was an exact copy of every other evening party, complete with talk, tea, and lit candles.

Before long Boris, Berg's old army friend, arrived. There was a shade of condescension and patronage in his treatment of Berg and Vera. After Boris came a lady with a colonel, then the general himself, then the Rostovs, and the party became indisputably just like every other evening party. Berg and Vera could not suppress their smiles of satisfaction at the sight of all this activity in their drawing room — the buzz of disconnected talk, the rustle of dresses, the bowing and scraping. Everything was just as everyone always has it — especially the general, who admired the apartment, patted Berg on the shoulder, and with paternal authority oversaw the setting up of the card table for boston. The general sat down beside Count Ilya Rostov, who was the next most important guest after himself. The older people sat with the older people, the young with the young, and the hostess presided over the tea table, which featured exactly the same kind of cakes in a silver basket as the Panins had at their parties. Everything was just as it was everywhere else.

chapters.title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 21
paragraphs: Pierre, as one of the principal guests, had to sit down to boston with Count Rostov, the general, and the colonel. At the card table he happened to be sitting directly across from Natasha, and was struck by a curious change that had come over her since the ball. She was quiet, and not only less pretty than at the ball, but saved from plainness only by her expression of gentle indifference to everything around her.

"What's the matter with her?" thought Pierre, glancing at her. She was sitting beside her sister at the tea table and reluctantly, without looking at him, responded to Boris, who had sat down next to her. After playing out a whole suit and, to his partner's delight, taking five tricks, Pierre heard greetings and footsteps as someone entered the room while he was gathering his cards. He glanced again at Natasha.
"What has happened to her?" he asked himself with even greater surprise.

Prince Andrew was standing before her, saying something to her with a look of tender concern. She had raised her head and was gazing up at him, flushed and clearly trying to control her rapid breathing. And the bright glow of some inner fire that had been suppressed was burning in her again. She was completely transformed — from a plain girl back into what she had been at the ball.
Prince Andrew went up to Pierre, and Pierre noticed a new and youthful expression on his friend's face.
Pierre changed seats several times during the game — sitting now with his back to Natasha, now facing her — but throughout all six rubbers he kept watching her and his friend.
"Something very important is happening between them," thought Pierre, and a feeling that was both joyful and painful stirred in him and made him neglect the game.

After six rubbers the general got up, declaring it was no use playing like that, and Pierre was free. Natasha was on one side of the room talking with Sonya and Boris, and Vera was saying something to Prince Andrew with a knowing smile. Pierre went up to his friend and, asking whether they were sharing secrets, sat down beside them. Vera, having noticed Prince Andrew's attention to Natasha, had decided that at a party — a real evening party — subtle allusions to romantic feelings were absolutely essential, and seizing a moment when Prince Andrew was alone she had started a conversation about feelings in general and about her sister. With such an intellectual guest as she considered Prince Andrew to be, she felt she needed to employ all her diplomatic skill.
When Pierre joined them he noticed that Vera was getting carried away by her own self-satisfied talk, while Prince Andrew looked embarrassed — something that rarely happened with him.

"What do you think?" Vera was saying with a sly smile. "You're so perceptive, Prince — you understand people's characters so well at a glance. What do you think of Natalie? Could she be constant in her attachments? Could she, like other women" — Vera meant herself — "love a man once and for all and remain true to him forever? That is what I consider true love. What do you think, Prince?"

"I know your sister too little," replied Prince Andrew with a sardonic smile meant to hide his discomfort, "to answer such a delicate question. And besides, I've noticed that the less attractive a woman is, the more constant she tends to be," he added, and looked up at Pierre, who was just approaching.

"Yes, that's true, Prince. In our day," continued Vera — using the phrase "our day" the way people of limited intelligence love to do, imagining they have discovered and assessed the special qualities of "our day," as if human nature changes with the times — "in our day a girl has so much freedom that the pleasure of being courted often smothers real feeling. And I must admit that Natalie is very susceptible." This return to the topic of Natasha made Prince Andrew frown uncomfortably; he was about to stand up, but Vera went on with an even subtler smile:

"I think no one has been more courted than she," she continued, "but until quite recently she never cared seriously for anyone. Now you know, Count," she said to Pierre, "even our dear cousin Boris, who between ourselves was very far gone in the land of tender feelings..." — alluding to a popular map of love that was in fashion at the time.
Prince Andrew frowned and said nothing.
"You're friendly with Boris, aren't you?" asked Vera.
"Yes, I know him..."
"I'm sure he's told you about his childhood love for Natasha?"
"Oh, there was a childhood romance?" Prince Andrew asked suddenly, blushing unexpectedly.
"Yes, you know — between cousins, closeness often leads to love. Le cousinage est un dangereux voisinage — cousinhood is a dangerous neighborhood, don't you think?"
* "Cousinhood is a dangerous neighborhood."

"Oh, absolutely!" said Prince Andrew, and with sudden, unnatural energy he began teasing Pierre about the need to be very careful with his fifty-year-old Moscow cousins. In the middle of these jokes he stood up, took Pierre by the arm, and drew him aside.
"Well?" asked Pierre, surprised by his friend's strange animation and noticing the glance he directed at Natasha as he rose.

"I must... I must talk to you," said Prince Andrew. "You know those women's gloves?" — he was referring to the Masonic gloves given to a newly initiated Brother, to be presented to the woman he loved. "I... but no, I'll tell you later..." and with a strange light in his eyes and a restlessness in his movements, Prince Andrew went over to Natasha and sat down beside her. Pierre watched as Prince Andrew asked her something and she blushed as she replied.
But at that moment Berg came up to Pierre and insisted that he join a debate between the general and the colonel about affairs in Spain.

Berg was satisfied and happy. The smile of pleasure never left his face. The party was a great success and exactly like other parties he had attended. Everything was just right: the ladies' subtle conversation, the cards, the general raising his voice at the card table, the samovar and the tea cakes. Only one thing was still missing — the thing he had always noticed at the evening parties he wanted to emulate. They hadn't yet had a loud, lively discussion among the men about something important and clever. Now the general had started just such a discussion, and so Berg pulled Pierre into it.

chapters.title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 22
paragraphs: The next day, having been invited by the count, Prince Andrew dined with the Rostovs and spent the rest of the day there.

Everyone in the house sensed for whose sake Prince Andrew kept coming, and without pretending otherwise, he tried to be near Natasha all day. Not only in the soul of the frightened yet happy and enraptured Natasha, but throughout the whole house, there was a feeling of awe — as though something important and inevitable was about to happen. The countess looked at Prince Andrew with sad, solemnly serious eyes when he talked to Natasha, and timidly launched into some artificial small talk whenever he glanced her way. Sonya was afraid to leave Natasha alone with him and equally afraid of being in the way. Natasha went pale with nervous anticipation whenever she found herself alone with him for a moment. His shyness astonished her. She felt that he wanted to say something but couldn't bring himself to do it.
That evening, when Prince Andrew had left, the countess went up to Natasha and whispered: "Well, what?"
"Mama! For heaven's sake, don't ask me anything now! One can't talk about it," said Natasha.

But all the same, that night, now agitated and now frightened, Natasha lay for a long time in her mother's bed, staring straight ahead. She told her how he had complimented her, how he'd mentioned going abroad, how he'd asked where they planned to spend the summer, and then how he'd asked about Boris.

"But such a thing... such a thing has never happened to me before!" she said. "Only I feel afraid when I'm with him. I'm always afraid. What does that mean? Does it mean it's the real thing? Yes? Mama, are you asleep?"
"No, my love; I'm frightened myself," answered her mother. "Now go to sleep!"

"I won't be able to sleep anyway. What silliness — to sleep! Mama! Mama! Nothing like this has ever happened to me before," she said, surprised and alarmed by the feeling she was aware of in herself. "And could we ever have imagined!..."

It seemed to Natasha that even the first time she had seen Prince Andrew at Otradnoe she had fallen in love with him. It was as if she feared this strange, unexpected happiness of meeting again the very man she had chosen then — she was firmly convinced she had — and finding him, it seemed, not indifferent to her.

"And it had to happen that he should come to Petersburg while we were here. And it had to happen that we should meet at that ball. It's fate. Clearly it's fate — everything was leading up to this! From the very first moment I saw him I felt something special."
"What else did he say to you? What are those poems? Read them..." said her mother, thinking it over, referring to some verses Prince Andrew had written in Natasha's album.
"Mama, does it matter that he's a widower?"
"Don't, Natasha! Pray to God. 'Marriages are made in heaven,'" said her mother.
"Darling Mama, how I love you! How happy I am!" cried Natasha, shedding tears of joy and excitement and hugging her mother.
At that very moment Prince Andrew was sitting with Pierre, telling him of his love for Natasha and his firm resolve to make her his wife.

That day Countess Helene had a reception at her house. The French ambassador was there, and a foreign prince of the blood who had recently become a frequent visitor, along with many brilliant ladies and gentlemen. Pierre, who had come downstairs, walked through the rooms and struck everyone by his preoccupied, absent-minded, and gloomy air.

Since the ball he had felt the approach of a spell of nervous depression and had been fighting desperately against it. Since the intimacy between his wife and the royal prince, Pierre had unexpectedly been made a gentleman of the bedchamber, and from that time he had begun to feel oppressed and ashamed in court society, and dark thoughts about the vanity of all things came to him more often than before. At the same time, the connection he had noticed between his protegee Natasha and Prince Andrew intensified his gloom by the contrast between his own situation and his friend's. He tried equally hard not to think about his wife, about Natasha, or about Prince Andrew; and yet everything seemed trivial compared with eternity. Again the question kept presenting itself: Why? What for? And he forced himself to work day and night at Masonic studies, hoping to drive away the dark spirit that threatened him. Toward midnight, after he had left the countess's apartments, he was sitting upstairs in a shabby dressing gown, copying out the original documents of the Scottish lodge of Freemasons at a table in his low, smoke-filled room, when someone came in. It was Prince Andrew.

"Ah, it's you!" said Pierre with a preoccupied, dissatisfied look. "And here I am, you see, hard at work." He pointed to his manuscript book with that air of seeking escape from life's troubles with which unhappy people regard their work.
Prince Andrew, with a beaming, ecstatic expression of renewed life on his face, stopped in front of Pierre and, not noticing his sad expression, smiled at him with the self-absorption of joy.
"Well, my dear friend," he said, "I wanted to tell you yesterday and I've come to do it now. I've never felt anything like this before. I am in love, my friend!"
Suddenly Pierre heaved a deep sigh and sank his heavy body down on the sofa beside Prince Andrew.
"With Natasha Rostova, yes?" he said.

"Yes, yes! Who else? I would never have believed it, but this feeling is stronger than I am. Yesterday I tortured myself, I suffered, but I wouldn't trade even that torment for anything in the world. I have not lived until now. Only now am I truly alive, but I can't live without her... But can she love me? I'm too old for her... Why don't you say something?"

"I? I? What did I tell you?" said Pierre, suddenly jumping up and pacing the room. "I always thought so... That girl is such a treasure... she is a rare girl... My dear friend, I beg you, don't analyze it, don't doubt it — marry, marry, marry!... And I'm sure there won't be a happier man on earth than you."
"But what about her?"
"She loves you."
"Don't talk nonsense..." said Prince Andrew, smiling and looking into Pierre's eyes.
"She does — I know it," Pierre declared fiercely.
"But listen," said Prince Andrew, catching him by the arm. "Do you know what state I'm in? I have to talk to someone about this."

"Well, go on, go on. I'm very glad," said Pierre, and his face really did change — his brow smoothed out and he listened to Prince Andrew with evident pleasure. Prince Andrew seemed, and truly was, a completely different, brand-new man. Where was his world-weariness, his contempt for life, his disillusionment? Pierre was the only person he had decided to confide in openly, and to him he poured out everything that was in his soul. Now he boldly and freely made plans for an expansive future, said he could not sacrifice his own happiness to his father's whims, and spoke of how he would either win his father's consent to the marriage and his love for Natasha, or manage without that consent. He marveled at the feeling that had taken hold of him, as at something strange, separate from and independent of himself.

"I wouldn't have believed anyone who told me I was capable of such love," said Prince Andrew. "It's not at all the same feeling I knew before. The whole world is now divided into two halves for me: one half is her, and there all is joy, hope, light; the other half is everything where she is not, and there all is gloom and darkness..."
"Gloom and darkness," repeated Pierre. "Yes, yes — I understand that."
"I can't help loving the light — it's not my fault. And I am very happy! You understand me? I know you're glad for my sake."
"Yes, yes," Pierre agreed, gazing at his friend with a moved and sorrowful expression. The brighter Prince Andrew's future appeared, the darker his own seemed.

chapters.title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 23
paragraphs: Prince Andrew needed his father's consent to the marriage, and the next day he set off for the country to obtain it.

His father received his son's news with outward calm but inner fury. He could not understand how anyone could wish to change his life or introduce anything new when his own life was already nearing its end. "If only they would let me finish my days in peace," the old man thought, "then they can do as they please." With his son, however, he employed the diplomacy he reserved for important occasions and, adopting a calm tone, discussed the whole matter.

First of all, the marriage was not a brilliant one as regards birth, wealth, or rank. Second, Prince Andrew was no longer young, and his health was poor — the old man stressed this particularly — while she was very young. Third, he had a son whom it would be a pity to entrust to a slip of a girl. "Fourth and finally," the father said, looking at his son with irony, "I ask you to put it off for a year. Go abroad, take a cure, find a German tutor for little Nicholas as you planned. Then if your love or passion or stubbornness — call it what you will — is still as strong, marry! And that's my last word on it. Remember — the last..." the prince concluded, in a tone that made clear nothing would change his mind.

Prince Andrew could see clearly that the old man hoped either his feelings or his fiancee's would not survive a year's test, or that he himself would die before then. He decided to comply with his father's wish — to propose and postpone the wedding for a year.
Three weeks after his last evening with the Rostovs, Prince Andrew returned to Petersburg.

The day after her conversation with her mother, Natasha waited for Bolkonski all day, but he didn't come. It was the same on the second and third days. Pierre didn't come either, and Natasha, not knowing that Prince Andrew had gone to see his father, could not explain his absence.

Three weeks went by like this. Natasha had no desire to go out anywhere and drifted from room to room like a shadow, idle and listless; she cried in secret at night and no longer came to her mother in the evenings. She blushed constantly and was irritable. It seemed to her that everyone knew about her disappointment and was laughing at her and pitying her. As strong as her inner grief was, this wound to her vanity only made her misery worse.
Once she came to her mother, tried to say something, and suddenly burst into tears. Her tears were those of an offended child who doesn't understand why it's being punished.
The countess began to comfort Natasha, who at first listened to her mother's words but then suddenly cut her off:
"Stop it, Mama! I don't think about it and I don't want to think about it! He just came and then stopped, stopped..."
Her voice trembled and she nearly cried again, but she recovered and went on quietly:
"And I don't want to get married at all. And I'm afraid of him; I've become quite calm now, quite calm."

The day after this conversation Natasha put on an old dress that she knew had the special property of making her feel cheerful in the morning, and that day she returned to the old way of life she had abandoned since the ball. After morning tea she went to the ballroom, which she particularly loved for its resonant acoustics, and began singing her vocal exercises. When she finished her first exercise she stopped in the middle of the room and sang a musical phrase that especially pleased her. She listened joyfully — as though she hadn't expected it — to the charm of the notes reverberating, filling the whole empty ballroom, and slowly dying away; and all at once she felt cheerful. "What's the point of making such a fuss about it? Things are perfectly fine as they are," she told herself, and she began pacing the room — not simply walking on the resonant parquet but stepping with each step from heel to toe, in a new and favorite pair of shoes, and listening to the rhythmic tap of the heel and creak of the toe with as much pleasure as she had listened to her own singing. Passing a mirror she glanced into it. "There — that's me!" her expression seemed to say. "Well, and very nice too! I don't need anybody."

A footman tried to come in to clear something from the room, but she wouldn't let him. Having shut the door behind him, she continued her walk. That morning she had returned to her favorite mood — love of and delight in herself. "What a charming girl that Natasha is!" she said again, speaking as if she were some third, collective, male person. "Pretty, a good voice, young, and not in anyone's way if only they'd leave her alone." But however much she was left alone, she couldn't be at peace now, and she immediately sensed this.

In the hall the front door opened, and someone asked "Is the family at home?" and then there were footsteps. Natasha was looking in the mirror but didn't see herself. She was listening to the sounds in the hall. When she caught sight of her own face, it was pale. It was him. She was certain of it, though she could barely hear his voice through the closed doors.
Pale and agitated, Natasha ran into the drawing room.
"Mama! Bolkonski is here!" she said. "Mama, this is terrible, it's unbearable! I don't want... to be tormented! What am I supposed to do?..."

Before the countess could answer, Prince Andrew entered the room with an agitated, serious face. The moment he saw Natasha his face brightened. He kissed the countess's hand and Natasha's and sat down beside the sofa.
"It's been so long since we had the pleasure..." the countess began, but Prince Andrew interrupted her by answering her intended question, clearly in a hurry to say what he had come to say.

"I haven't been to see you all this time because I was at my father's. I needed to discuss a very important matter with him. I only got back last night," he said, glancing at Natasha. "I need to speak with you, Countess," he added after a moment's pause.
The countess lowered her eyes, sighing deeply.
"I am at your disposal," she murmured.
Natasha knew she ought to leave, but couldn't. Something gripped her throat, and ignoring all propriety she stared straight at Prince Andrew with wide-open eyes.
"Now? This very instant?... No, it can't be!" she thought.
He glanced at her again, and that glance convinced her she was not mistaken. Yes — right now, this very instant, her fate would be decided.
"Go, Natasha! I'll call you," said the countess in a whisper.
Natasha looked at Prince Andrew and at her mother with frightened, imploring eyes and went out.
"I have come, Countess, to ask for your daughter's hand," said Prince Andrew.
The countess's face flushed hotly, but she said nothing.

"Your offer..." she began at last, speaking with an effort at composure. He remained silent, looking into her eyes. "Your offer..." she grew confused, "is welcome to us, and I accept your offer. I am glad. And my husband... I hope... but it will depend on her..."
"I will speak to her when I have your consent... Do you give it to me?" said Prince Andrew.

"Yes," replied the countess. She held out her hand to him, and with a mingled feeling of strangeness and tenderness pressed her lips to his forehead as he stooped to kiss her hand. She wanted to love him as a son but felt he was a stranger, a daunting man. "I'm sure my husband will agree," said the countess, "but your father..."
"My father, to whom I have told my plans, has made it an express condition that the wedding not take place for a year. And I wanted to tell you of that," said Prince Andrew.
"It's true that Natasha is still young, but — that long?..."
"It can't be helped," said Prince Andrew with a sigh.
"I will send her to you," said the countess, and left the room.
"Lord have mercy on us!" she repeated as she went to find her daughter.

Sonya said Natasha was in her bedroom. Natasha was sitting on the bed, pale and dry-eyed, staring at the icons and whispering something as she rapidly crossed herself. Seeing her mother she jumped up and flew to her.
"Well, Mama?... Well?..."
"Go, go to him. He is asking for your hand," said the countess, coldly it seemed to Natasha. "Go... go," said the mother, sadly and reproachfully, with a deep sigh, as her daughter rushed away.

Natasha never remembered how she entered the drawing room. When she walked in and saw him, she stopped. "Is it possible that this stranger has now become everything to me?" she asked herself, and immediately answered: "Yes, everything! He alone is now dearer to me than everything in the world." Prince Andrew came toward her with lowered eyes.
"I have loved you from the very first moment I saw you. May I hope?"
He looked at her and was struck by the serious, passionate expression on her face. Her face said: "Why ask? Why doubt what you cannot help but know? Why put into words what words can never express?"
She moved closer to him and stopped. He took her hand and kissed it.
"Do you love me?"
"Yes, yes!" Natasha whispered, almost crossly. Then she sighed deeply and, catching her breath faster and faster, began to sob.
"What is it? What's the matter?"
"Oh, I'm so happy!" she answered, smiled through her tears, leaned closer to him, paused for a moment as if asking herself whether she might, and then kissed him.

Prince Andrew held her hands, looked into her eyes, and did not find in his heart his former love for her. Something in him had suddenly changed; there was no longer the old poetic and mystical pull of desire, but instead pity for her feminine and childish vulnerability, awe at her devotion and trust, and a heavy yet joyful sense of the duty that now bound him to her forever. The present feeling, though not as bright and poetic as the earlier one, was stronger and more serious.
"Did your mother tell you it cannot be for a year?" asked Prince Andrew, still looking into her eyes.

"Is it possible that I — the 'little girl,' as everyone called me," thought Natasha, "is it possible that I am now to be the wife and equal of this strange, dear, clever man whom even my father looks up to? Can it be true? Can it be true that there can be no more playing at life, that now I am grown up, that I am responsible for my every word and deed? Yes, but what did he just ask me?"
"No," she replied, but she hadn't understood his question.
"Forgive me," he said. "But you are so young, and I have already been through so much. I am afraid for you — you don't yet know yourself."
Natasha listened with intense concentration, trying but failing to grasp the meaning of his words.

"Difficult as this year of delay will be — the year that postpones my happiness," continued Prince Andrew, "it will give you time to be sure of yourself. I ask you to make me happy in a year, but you are free: our engagement shall remain a secret, and should you find that you don't love me, or should you come to love..." said Prince Andrew with a forced smile.
"Why do you say that?" Natasha interrupted. "You know that from the very day you first came to Otradnoe I have loved you," she cried, completely convinced she was speaking the truth.
"In a year you will learn to know yourself..."
"A whole year!" Natasha repeated suddenly, only now grasping that the wedding was to be postponed for a year. "But why a year? Why a year?..."
Prince Andrew began to explain the reasons for the delay. Natasha didn't hear him.
"And there's no way around it?" she asked. Prince Andrew did not answer, but his face made clear that the decision could not be changed.

"It's awful! Oh, it's awful! Awful!" Natasha suddenly cried, and burst into sobs again. "I'll die waiting a year — it's impossible, it's awful!" She looked into her lover's face and saw in it an expression of sympathy and bewilderment.
"No, no! I'll do anything!" she said, suddenly stopping her tears. "I'm so happy."
The father and mother came into the room and gave the engaged couple their blessing.
From that day Prince Andrew began coming to the Rostovs' as Natasha's fiance.

chapters.title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 24
paragraphs: There was no formal betrothal ceremony, and Natasha's engagement to Bolkonski was not announced; Prince Andrew insisted on this. He said that since he was responsible for the delay, he alone should bear the burden of it; that he had given his word and was bound forever, but that he didn't wish to bind Natasha and was giving her complete freedom. If after six months she felt she didn't love him, she would have every right to reject him. Naturally neither Natasha nor her parents wanted to hear of this, but Prince Andrew was firm. He came to the Rostovs' every day, but didn't behave toward Natasha as an engaged man: he didn't use the intimate "thou" but addressed her as "you," and kissed only her hand. After the engagement, completely different relations sprang up between them — intimate, natural, and sincere. It was as if they hadn't known each other before. Both loved to recall how they had thought of each other when they were still nothing to one another; they felt themselves now to be entirely different people — then they had been artificial, now they were natural and genuine. At first the family felt somewhat constrained around Prince Andrew; he seemed like a man from another world. For a long time Natasha had to train the family to get used to him, proudly assuring them all that he only seemed different but was really just like everyone else, and that she wasn't afraid of him and nobody else should be either. After a few days they grew accustomed to him and went on with their usual way of life in his presence, and he took part in it. He could talk about estate management with the count, about fashion with the countess and Natasha, and about albums and needlework with Sonya. Sometimes the household, both among themselves and in his presence, marveled at how it had all come about and at the obvious signs that had foretold it: Prince Andrew's visit to Otradnoe, their coming to Petersburg, the resemblance between Natasha and Prince Andrew that the old nurse had noticed on his first visit, and Andrew's encounter with Nicholas in 1805, and many other incidents that seemed to prove it was all meant to be.

In the house that poetic stillness and quiet reigned which always accompanies the presence of an engaged couple. Often when they were all sitting together everyone would fall silent. Sometimes the others would get up and leave, and the couple, left alone, would still remain silent. They rarely spoke of their future life. Prince Andrew was afraid and ashamed to bring it up. Natasha shared this feeling, as she did all his feelings, which she constantly intuited. Once she began asking about his son. Prince Andrew blushed, as he often did now — Natasha especially loved this in him — and said that his son would not live with them.
"Why not?" asked Natasha, alarmed.
"I can't take him away from his grandfather, and besides..."
"How I would have loved him!" said Natasha, instantly guessing his thought. "But I understand — you want to avoid giving anyone a reason to criticize us."

Sometimes the old count would come over, kiss Prince Andrew, and ask his advice about Petya's education or Nicholas's career. The old countess would sigh as she looked at them; Sonya kept getting nervous that she was in the way and tried to find excuses to leave them alone, even when they didn't want her to. When Prince Andrew spoke — and he could tell a story very well — Natasha listened with pride; when she spoke, she noticed with a mixture of fear and joy that he watched her attentively and searchingly. She asked herself in bewilderment: "What is he looking for in me? He's trying to find something by studying me! What if what he seeks isn't there?" Sometimes she fell into one of the wild, giddy moods that were so characteristic of her, and then she particularly loved to watch how Prince Andrew laughed. He laughed rarely, but when he did, he gave himself over to it completely, and after such laughter she always felt closer to him. Natasha would have been perfectly happy if the thought of the approaching separation had not terrified her, just as the mere thought of it made him turn pale and cold.

On the eve of his departure from Petersburg, Prince Andrew brought Pierre along. Pierre had not been to the Rostovs' once since the ball. He seemed distracted and embarrassed. He was talking to the countess, and Natasha sat down at a little chess table with Sonya, silently inviting Prince Andrew to come too. He did so.
"You've known Bezukhov a long time?" he asked. "Do you like him?"
"Yes, he's a dear, but very funny."
And as usual when talking about Pierre, she began telling stories of his absent-mindedness, some of which had even been made up about him.

"Do you know, I've told him our secret? I've known him since childhood. He has a heart of gold. I beg you, Natalie," Prince Andrew said with sudden seriousness, "I'm going away, and heaven knows what may happen. You may stop loving... All right, I know I'm not supposed to say that. Just this, then: whatever may happen to you when I'm not here..."
"What could happen?"

"Whatever trouble may come," Prince Andrew continued, "I beg you, Mademoiselle Sophie, whatever happens, turn to him alone for advice and help! He's the most absent-minded and absurd fellow, but he has a heart of gold."

Neither her father, nor her mother, nor Sonya, nor Prince Andrew himself could have predicted how the separation from her fiance would affect Natasha. Flushed and agitated, she went about the house all that day, dry-eyed, busying herself with the most trivial matters as if she didn't understand what was coming. She didn't even cry when, saying goodbye, he kissed her hand for the last time. "Don't go!" she said in a tone that made him wonder whether he really ought not to stay — and which he remembered long afterward. Nor did she cry when he was gone; but for several days she sat in her room, dry-eyed, taking no interest in anything, only saying now and then: "Oh, why did he go away?"

But two weeks after his departure, to the surprise of everyone around her, she recovered from her emotional illness just as suddenly, and became her old self again — though with a change in her inner character, as a child gets up after a long illness with a different expression on its face.

chapters.title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 25
paragraphs: During that year after his son's departure, old Prince Nicholas Bolkonski's health and temper grew much worse. He became still more irritable, and it was Princess Mary who usually bore the brunt of his frequent fits of unprovoked anger. He seemed to search deliberately for her most sensitive spots in order to torment her mentally as cruelly as possible. Princess Mary had two passions and therefore two sources of joy — her nephew, little Nicholas, and religion — and these were the old prince's favorite targets for mockery and attack. Whatever the topic of conversation, he would steer it around to the superstitions of old maids or the pampering and spoiling of children. "You want to turn him" — little Nicholas — "into an old maid like yourself! A pity! Prince Andrew wants a son, not an old maid," he would say. Or, turning to Mademoiselle Bourienne, he would ask her in Princess Mary's presence how she liked their village priests and icons, and would joke about them.

He continually hurt Princess Mary and tormented her, but it cost her no effort to forgive him. Could he really be to blame? Could her father, whom she knew loved her in spite of everything, truly be unjust? And what is justice? The princess never dwelt on that proud word "justice." All the complex laws of humanity were reduced for her into one clear and simple law — the law of love and self-sacrifice taught by Him who lovingly suffered for mankind though He Himself was God. What did she have to do with the justice or injustice of other people? She had to endure and love, and that is what she did.

During the winter Prince Andrew had come to Bald Hills and had been gay, gentle, and more affectionate than Princess Mary had known him in a long time. She felt that something had happened to him, but he told her nothing about his love. Before he left he had a long conversation with his father about something, and Princess Mary noticed that before his departure they were dissatisfied with one another.

Soon after Prince Andrew's departure, Princess Mary wrote to her friend Julie Karagina in Petersburg — the one she had dreamed, as all girls do, of marrying to her brother — who was at that time in mourning for her own brother, killed in Turkey.
Sorrow, it seems, is our common lot, my dear, tender friend Julie.

Your loss is so terrible that I can only explain it as a special act of God's providence — He who, loving you, wishes to try you and your excellent mother. Oh, my friend! Religion, and religion alone, can — I will not say comfort us — but save us from despair. Religion alone can explain what without its help we cannot comprehend: why kind and noble people who could find happiness in life — who harm no one and are necessary to the happiness of others — are called away to God, while cruel, useless, harmful people, or those who are a burden to themselves and to everyone around them, are left alive. The first death I ever witnessed, one I shall never forget — that of my dear sister-in-law — left that impression on me. Just as you ask fate why your wonderful brother had to die, so I asked why that angel Lise, who never wronged anyone and in whose soul there was never an unkind thought, had to die. And what do you think, dear friend? Five years have passed since then, and I, with my small understanding, am beginning to see clearly why she had to die, and in what way that death was an expression of the infinite goodness of the Creator, whose every action, though generally incomprehensible to us, is nothing but a manifestation of His infinite love for His creatures. Perhaps, I often think, she was too angelically innocent to have the strength to fulfill all a mother's duties. As a young wife she was irreproachable; perhaps she could not have been so as a mother. As it is, she has not only left us — and particularly Prince Andrew — with the purest memories and regrets, but she will likely receive there a place I dare not hope for myself. But to speak not of her alone — that early and terrible death has had the most beneficial influence on me and on my brother despite all our grief. Then, at the moment of our loss, these thoughts would never have occurred to me; I would have dismissed them with horror. But now they are very clear and certain. I write all this to you, dear friend, only to convince you of the Gospel truth which has become the guiding principle of my life: not a single hair of our heads will fall without His will. And His will is governed only by infinite love for us, and so whatever happens to us is for our good.

You ask whether we shall spend next winter in Moscow. Despite my wish to see you, I don't think so and don't want to. You will be surprised to hear that the reason is Bonaparte! Here is why: my father's health is growing noticeably worse; he cannot tolerate any contradiction and is becoming irritable. This irritability is, as you know, directed mainly at political matters. He cannot endure the idea that Bonaparte is negotiating on equal terms with all the sovereigns of Europe, and especially with ours, the grandson of the Great Catherine! As you know, I am quite indifferent to politics, but from my father's conversations and his talks with Michael Ivanovich I know everything that goes on in the world, and especially about the honors being heaped on Bonaparte — who, it seems, is accepted everywhere in the world as a great man and even Emperor of France, everywhere except at Bald Hills. And my father cannot bear it. It seems to me that it is mainly because of his political views that my father is reluctant to speak of going to Moscow; for he foresees the confrontations that would result from his habit of expressing his opinions without regard for anyone. Any benefit he might get from medical treatment he would lose in the arguments about Bonaparte that would be unavoidable. In any case the matter will be decided very soon.

Our family life goes on as before, except for my brother Andrew's absence. He, as I wrote to you before, has changed very much of late. After his grief, it was only this year that he truly recovered his spirits. He has become again as I knew him when we were children: kind, affectionate, with that heart of gold for which I know no equal. He has realized, it seems to me, that life is not over for him. But along with this inner change he has grown physically much weaker. He has become thinner and more nervous. I worry about him and am glad he is taking this trip abroad that his doctors have long recommended. I hope it will restore his health. You write that in Petersburg he is spoken of as one of the most active, cultivated, and capable of the young men. Forgive my family pride, but I never doubted it. The good he has done for everyone here, from his peasants to the gentry, is incalculable. On his arrival in Petersburg he received only his due. I am always amazed at the way rumors fly from Petersburg to Moscow, especially false ones such as the one you mention — that my brother is engaged to the little Rostova. I do not think my brother will ever marry again, and certainly not her; and this is why: first, I know that though he rarely speaks of the wife he lost, the grief of that loss has gone too deep in his heart for him ever to give her a successor and our little angel a stepmother. Second, as far as I know, that girl is not the kind who could please Prince Andrew. I do not think he would choose her for a wife, and frankly I would not wish it. But I am going on too long and am at the end of my second sheet. Goodbye, my dear friend. May God keep you in His holy and mighty care. My dear friend Mademoiselle Bourienne sends you kisses.
MARY

chapters.title: Book Seven (1810 - 11) — Chapter 26
paragraphs: In the middle of summer Princess Mary received an unexpected letter from Prince Andrew in Switzerland, containing strange and surprising news. He wrote of his engagement to Natasha Rostova. The entire letter breathed a loving rapture for his betrothed and a tender, confiding affection for his sister. He wrote that he had never loved as he did now and that only now did he understand what life truly was. He asked his sister to forgive him for not having told her of his decision during his last visit to Bald Hills, though he had discussed it with their father. He had not told her for fear she would ask their father for his consent, angering the old man and bearing the brunt of his displeasure without achieving anything. "Besides," he wrote, "the matter was not so definite then as it is now. Our father insisted on a year's delay, and now already six months — half the time — have passed, and my resolve is firmer than ever. If the doctors did not keep me here at the spa I would be back in Russia already, but as it is I must postpone my return for three months. You know me and my relationship with Father. I want nothing from him. I have always been and always shall be independent; but to go against his will and provoke his anger, when he may remain with us only a short time longer, would destroy half my happiness. I am now writing to him about the same matter, and I beg you to choose a good moment to give him my letter and let me know how he takes it, and whether there is any hope that he may agree to shorten the waiting period by four months."
After long hesitation, doubt, and prayer, Princess Mary gave the letter to her father. The next day the old prince said to her quietly:
"Write and tell your brother to wait until I'm dead... It won't be long — I'll set him free soon enough."
The princess tried to reply, but her father wouldn't let her speak and, raising his voice higher and higher, cried:

"Marry, marry, my boy!... A fine family!... Smart people, eh? Rich, eh? Yes, a nice stepmother for little Nicholas! Write and tell him he can marry tomorrow if he likes. She'll be little Nicholas's stepmother, and I'll marry Bourienne!... Ha, ha, ha! He shouldn't be without a stepmother either! Only one thing — no more women in my house. Let him marry and live on his own. Maybe you'd like to go live with him too?" he added, turning to Princess Mary. "Go right ahead! Out into the cold... the cold... the cold!"

After this outburst the prince did not raise the subject again. But his suppressed fury at his son's weak-willed behavior found expression in his treatment of his daughter. To his former pretexts for mockery a new one was added — pointed references to stepmothers and conspicuous courtesies toward Mademoiselle Bourienne.
"Why shouldn't I marry her?" he asked his daughter. "She'll make a splendid princess!"

And lately, to her surprise and bewilderment, Princess Mary noticed that her father really was associating more and more with the Frenchwoman. She wrote to Prince Andrew about their father's reaction but tried to comfort him with hopes of a reconciliation.

Little Nicholas and his education, her brother Andrew, and religion were Princess Mary's joys and consolations; but besides these, since everyone must have personal hopes, Princess Mary had a hidden dream deep in her heart that provided the chief comfort of her life. This comforting dream and hope were given to her by God's folk — the half-witted wanderers and other pilgrims who visited her without the prince's knowledge. The longer she lived and the more she saw of life, the greater was her wonder at the shortsightedness of people who seek pleasure and happiness on this earth: toiling, suffering, struggling, and harming one another to attain an impossible, illusory, sinful happiness. Prince Andrew had loved his wife — she died, but that was not enough: he wanted to bind his happiness to another woman. Her father objected because he wanted a more distinguished and wealthy match for Andrew. And they all struggled and suffered and tormented one another and damaged their eternal souls, all for the sake of benefits that last no more than an instant. Not only do we know this ourselves, but Christ, the Son of God, came down to earth and told us that this life is but a moment, a trial; yet we cling to it and think to find happiness in it. "How is it that no one sees this?" thought Princess Mary. "No one except these despised holy wanderers who, with knapsack on their backs, come to me by the back door, afraid of being seen by the prince — not from fear of mistreatment but to save him from sin. To leave family, home, and all worldly cares, to wander in rough garments from place to place under an assumed name, doing no one any harm but praying for all — for those who drive one away as well as for those who shelter one: there is no life or truth higher than that!"

There was one pilgrim, a quiet, pockmarked little woman of about fifty named Theodosia, who for over thirty years had walked barefoot and worn heavy chains. Princess Mary was especially fond of her. Once, when they sat together in a dimly lit room before an icon, Theodosia was telling the story of her life, and the thought suddenly came to Princess Mary with overwhelming force that Theodosia alone had found the true path. She resolved then and there to become a pilgrim herself. She confided this idea to no one except her confessor, Father Akinfi the monk, who approved. Under the guise of a gift for the pilgrims, Princess Mary prepared a complete pilgrim's outfit for herself: a rough shirt, bast shoes, a coarse coat, and a black kerchief. Often, approaching the chest of drawers that held this secret treasure, Princess Mary would pause, wondering whether the time had come to put her plan into action.

Often, listening to the pilgrims' stories, she was so moved by their simple words — mechanical to them but full of deep meaning for her — that several times she was on the point of abandoning everything and running away from home. In her imagination she already saw herself beside Theodosia, dressed in coarse rags, walking with a staff and a knapsack on her back along a dusty road, making her way from one holy shrine to another, free from envy, earthly love, or desire, and reaching at last the place where there is no more sorrow or sighing, but eternal joy and bliss.

"I shall come to a place and pray there, and before I have time to get attached to it or love it, I shall move on. I will keep walking until my legs give way, and I'll lie down and die somewhere, and at last reach that eternal, peaceful haven where there is neither sorrow nor sighing..." thought Princess Mary.

But afterward, when she saw her father and especially little Koko — Nicholas — her resolve would weaken. She would weep quietly and feel that she was a sinner who loved her father and her little nephew more than she loved God.
